https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 Statement on Automated Takedown of Its Instagram Posts by Meta

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restriction of its Instagram post discussing the censorship faced by digital fact-checking organisation Alt News, as well as the subsequent takedown of an Instagram Story in which https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 on 17th September 2026 had published a post highlighting the takedowns faced by Alt News in relation to its reporting on the Chauhaan film teaser. Alt News on 19th August 2026 had published a report on the content takedown they had faced, which was as follows. An Instagram post by Alt News based on the analysis of the teaser of the movie ‘Chauhaan’ was restricted by Instagram. A subsequent version was also removed, while a third version, after references to Hizbul Mujahideen militant “Burhan Wani” were removed, was allowed to remain online. Alt News also stated that search results for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram yielded no results and instead showed a message that said “these search terms may be associated with socially sensitive content”.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has been actively monitoring content takedowns through its Free Speech Tracker and had written extensively about the restrictions faced by Alt News and made a social media post discussing these particular instances to highlight the growing use of opaque content moderation systems on platforms and the chilling effect such systems can have on journalism and public-interest speech. The post specifically noted that such censorship can operate even without a formal government order, and that journalists may begin self-censoring if they believe that certain subjects, words or images could trigger restrictions.

Instagram subsequently restricted https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s posts in India. The notification stated that the content was restricted through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.” The matter became even more concerning when Scroll reported on the restrictions faced by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 and Alt News in a post on Instagram. When https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 shared Scroll’s report on the matter through an Instagram Story on its public handle, the Story was also taken down by Instagram through the use of automated systems.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 is deeply concerned about the increasing reliance on automated systems for implementing content restrictions and legal compliance requirements. The lack of clarity around this notification further adds to the concern. Since the content has been taken down by automated systems it is unclear whether the restriction stems from a specific legal request or order issued to Meta, or whether Meta has restricted the content suo motu through its automated systems as part of its compliance with the due diligence requirements under the Information Technology Rules, 2021. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has not been provided with sufficient information to determine the source of the restriction, the specific legal basis for it, or the process through which the decision can be challenged.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 emphasises that journalists and news outlets are facing systemic suppression due to over-automated content moderation systems that lack context for investigative reporting, public interest documentation, and critical commentary. By conflating legitimate reporting on sensitive or controversial issues with violations of Community Standards or legal requirements through automated moderation, Meta effectively silences public-interest journalism without human oversight. This opaque suppression undermines press freedom, as well as the public’s right to reliable information, and leaves users without timely recourse to contest improper takedowns.

This situation is exacerbated by the fact that the official Grievance Officer intake form for reporting does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements”. The response from the Meta AI support assistant instead asks users to physically send an email to the resident Grievance Officer, creating an entirely separate standard for reporting content takedown as opposed to other grievances. As per the Meta platforms the email available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Office report. This not only creates excessive additional friction for users, but in the case of news reporting, effectively silences journalists and curbs the spread of information for significant periods of time. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon Meta to restore https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s post with immediate effect and provide a clear explanation of the legal basis for the takedown. Meta must also ensure meaningful human oversight for restrictions and provide users with an effective and timely mechanism to challenge erroneous takedown especially if done by automated systems. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions and to clarify whether restrictions were imposed pursuant to government or law-enforcement requests or through Meta’s own systems. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible and timely avenues to contest takedowns.

text:
Digital rights group says its post about Instagram blocking ‘Alt News’ posts has been blocked

https://t.co/YFF4QsTHld

It referred to a story by the factchecker that mentioned Hizbul Mujahideen militant Burhan Wani.

The Internet Freedom Foundation stands with https://t.co/eAhBlCEUwk against Meta’s restriction in India of its Instagram post documenting content takedowns affecting Alt News. Three of the post’s five slides, mentioning “Burhan Wani”, were withheld by automated systems. Only two remain visible in India. Meta’s notice identifies neither the Community Standard nor the legal provision relied upon, and provides no explanation of how to challenge the restriction.

Documenting censorship is an exercise of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). Unexplained restrictions on such reporting undermine access to information and discourage journalists, researchers and civil society from discussing matters of public interest. Automated moderation must account for context and distinguish documentation from endorsement.

Meta must provide specific reasons for its decisions, disclose whether restrictions arise from its policies or a government or court direction, and explain the role of automated systems. Affected users must have access to meaningful, time-bound review, including human assessment and restoration where a restriction is unjustified. These are basic safeguards against arbitrary restrictions on expression.

We call on Meta to restore the withheld slides unless it can substantiate a legitimate, clearly disclosed basis for restricting them, and to explain the policy and process applied. Reporting on censorship must not become a further target of opaque platform decisions.

IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

The Internet Freedom Foundation stands with https://t.co/eAhBlCEUwk against Meta’s restriction in India of its Instagram post documenting content takedowns affecting Alt News. Three of the post’s five slides, mentioning “Burhan Wani”, were withheld by automated systems. Only two remain visible in India. Meta’s notice identifies neither the Community Standard nor the legal provision relied upon, and provides no explanation of how to challenge the restriction.

Documenting censorship is an exercise of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). Unexplained restrictions on such reporting undermine access to information and discourage journalists, researchers and civil society from discussing matters of public interest. Automated moderation must account for context and distinguish documentation from endorsement.

Meta must provide specific reasons for its decisions, disclose whether restrictions arise from its policies or a government or court direction, and explain the role of automated systems. Affected users must have access to meaningful, time-bound review, including human assessment and restoration where a restriction is unjustified. These are basic safeguards against arbitrary restrictions on expression.

We call on Meta to restore the withheld slides unless it can substantiate a legitimate, clearly disclosed basis for restricting them, and to explain the policy and process applied. Reporting on censorship must not become a further target of opaque platform decisions.

text:
A stand-up comedian had two of his original Instagram reels removed after anonymous accounts filed copyright complaints using the same generic Turkish-language text, without identifying any allegedly infringed work. It took a Delhi High Court case for Meta to restore both reels. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/RukNwsovEw

But restoration is not the end of the issue. The High Court order does not record that the copyright strikes themselves have been expunged. The questions of removing those strikes and preventing Meta from taking adverse action against Pulkit's page on their basis remain before the Court. (9/10)

This case shows what happens when copyright enforcement becomes the easiest route to getting content removed. A platform says complaints are reviewed and only valid reports are acted upon. Yet two vague complaints were enough to remove content, while repeated appeals produced no reasoned response for months. If the correct decision could be reached once a case entered court, why was it unavailable through the platform's own grievance system?

IFF will continue pushing for meaningful verification of copyright claims, reasoned decisions on appeals within the IT Rules' timelines, and greater transparency around takedowns and reversals. (10/10)

There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. A jammer is a radio transmitter that can cut voice calls, SMS and mobile data for everyone within its range. So who gives the Delhi Police the power to switch one on? (1/10)

text:
There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. A jammer is a radio transmitter that can cut voice calls, SMS and mobile data for everyone within its range. So who gives the Delhi Police the power to switch one on? (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/kU0KOf2fOY

On 8 September, IFF filed three RTIs with the Delhi Police. We are seeking records on every jammer it possesses, the permissions and procurement documents, the officers authorised to deploy them, the applicable SOPs and deployment registers, and the specific records concerning Jantar Mantar on 20 and 22 July. We have also asked for the records behind the Satya Niketan denial. (9/10)

The question is not whether telecommunications can ever be restricted. Indian law already provides a framework for temporary suspension of services. The question is whether a separate, less visible mechanism can bypass those safeguards and cut communications without the written order, publication, review and accountability that accompany a lawful shutdown. IFF will publish the Delhi Police's replies, including any silence, and continue seeking clarity on who can jam communications, for what purpose and under what law. (10/10)

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)
